newsitem.title: UK: British PM tells Bosnians to abide by peace accord.
newsitem.headline: British PM tells Bosnians to abide by peace accord.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major opened an international conference on Bosnia on Wednesday by calling on its ethnic leaders to stick to the terms of the Dayton peace agreement which ended 43 months of war.
He said they should live up to the trust and expectations of the vast majority of Bosnians who wanted to live in peace.

The conference, bringing together foreign ministers from Europe, North America, Russia, Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia, as well as officials from the major aid agencies, was to discuss the problems during a Peace Implementation Conference which continues on Thursday.
In an opening speech, Major told Bosnia's leaders that although the Dayton peace agreement had achieved a great deal, much remained to be done.
"None of us at this conference underestimates the task you face. You are rebuilding a nation, only a few months after a bitter war, with the wounds and divisions not yet healed," he said.
"But you were elected by the Bosnian people as their investment in, and commitment to, a brighter future. They have placed their trust in you...this is a heavy responsibility."

British officials said the various sides were hampering freedom of movement, preventing refugees from returning home, committing human rights abuses, refusing to hand over indicted war criminals and not complying with agreed arms reductions.
Major held talks on Wednesday with Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's Moslem leader. He is one of three co-presidents along with Bosnian Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak.

Major said that Bosnian leaders would have to take difficult decisions and make difficult compromises and called on the three co-presidents to put the wider interests of their people above short-term concerns.

NATO has agreed to maintain an armed force in Bosnia for another 18 months to keep the former warring sides apart but the West fears that unless the country is rebuilt quickly, it will fall apart when Western troops leave.
Major told the Bosnian leaders that they would have to start doing more for themselves

"There is a limit to what the international community can do," Major said. "One year on from the signature of the peace agreement, ordinary Bosnians are still afraid to cross the line between the (Serb and Moslem-Croat) entities. This cannot continue."

He said all sides had to stick to arms control agreements. "The follow-up has been less than wholehearted. This cannot be allowed to slip. The international community is determined to maintain pressure on this issue until we have achieved our objectives."
He said that the West would be looking for a series of detailed political undertakings from the Bosnian leaders.

"The international community will in turn undertake to provide substantial further help and resources, both human and financial. But this international help will be conditional on the willingness in Bosnia and Herzegovina to implement all aspects of the peace agreement."
